newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Papua New Guinea crisis may upset economic progress.
newsitem.headline: Papua New Guinea crisis may upset economic progress.

text.p: Papua New Guinea, one of the South Pacific's most resource-rich economies, faces the prospect of renewed economic crisis if it is unable to secure a quick return to political stability, analysts say.

The country had only just recovered from its last crisis before lurching nine days ago into the political uproar over Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan's hiring of a mercenary force to counter independence fighters on Bougainville island.
"It (the economy) is very dynamic at the moment," PNG specialist Satish Chand of the Australian National University's National Centre for Development Studies said on Tuesday.
Chand believes the latest crisis has put Papua New Guinea at the brink of a potential capital outflow which could shake the nation's currency, the kina.

Other analysts, including John Millett, director of Port Moresby-based think tank, the Institute of National Affairs, believe the economy will survive unscathed from the present standoff between Chan and a rebellious military.
All views on Papua New Guinea's economy, however, agree that volatility is as much a characteristic as its reliance on copper, gold, energy and agricultural products led by coffee.
Rapid growth in gross domestic product (GDP) at the start of the 1990s collapsed into decline just a few years later before another turn-around led to more modest growth.
Fuelled by a booming extractive sector, GDP growth soared to 16.6 percent in 1993 before collapsing to 2.4 percent in 1994.
Major currency reform in late 1994 led to an economic contraction of 2.9 percent in 1995 before a return to moderate growth at 2.3 percent in 1996.
The country's economic prospects now depend on the balance which emerges between instability, primarily through potential capital outflow, and recently-improving economic figures.
Until a week ago, most economic indicators were positive and pointing to a convincing recovery from the more than 30 percent devaluation of the kina since late 1994.
Debt as a proportion of gross domestic product had been falling while GDP rose slightly, to 6.5 billion kina (US$4.7 billion) in 1996 from 6.4 billion kina the year before.

An increase in the country's outstanding debt, to 3.7 billion kina at September 30, 1996 from 3.3 billion kina in 1995, is seen by economists as more the result of the 1994 devaluation than of increased borrowing. Papua New Guinea's debt service ratio on export income has also been declining, despite a drop in exports to 3.1 billion kina in 1996 from 3.6 billion kina the year before.
"The economy's been expanding but we haven't been borrowing externally," Millett said.
Interest rates are down to 10 percent, half their peak after the 1994 devaluation, while inflation remains comparatively subdued at about 11 percent.

Employment has also been rising, largely in response to major infrastructure projects promoted by the Chan government, including a transnational highway, Port Moresby's airport project, and arterial roads.

Economists who hold strong fears over how Papua New Guinea's economy will cope with the current political crisis say the only relevant factor is stability. Who emerges as winner or loser, leader or vanquished, is irrelevant.
ANU's Chand said he believed some capital would have already left the country in response to the latest crisis.
"The uncertainty itself will have an impact. I'm pretty sure PNG would have lost a fair bit of foreign reserves by now," Chand told Reuters. Official figures do not exist.

Toward the end of 1996 PNG's reserves were estimated at more than 400 million kina, or about six months' worth of imports. Six months after the 1994 devaluation, reserves had shrunk so far as to only cover imports for a few days.
Fears also existed that the World Bank and IMF would withdraw support for Papua New Guinea if stability did not return, Chand said.
In the meantime, signs of a crunch for the economy would be strong capital outflow and a deferral of new projects, even though production might continue at existing projects, he said.
(One kina=US$0.72)
